Part of the superhero origin story is that Chaerephon, a friend of Socrates’, goes to the oracle and asks who the wisest man is, and the oracle says Socrates. So Socrates goes on a mission to figure out how this could be the case by interviewing the wisest people he knows. He begins with the politicians, then moves on to the poets, and ends with the artisans. In these interviews, he has a realization about the kind of wisdom that he has. This epiphany is one Socrates often has in the dialogues, including with the first politician he speaks to. He says, “For he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know.” Later in The Apology, he describes his wisdom as “a position between knowledge and ignorance.” What kind of a position is that for the interviewer or the questioner to assume?

It is very hard for the interviewee to put forward “I don’t know anything,” because I’ve got to answer your questions. Characteristically, that’s not Socrates’ role. He is usually the one asking the questions, but in this dialogue, he is answering for himself. There’s a sense in which the interviewee cannot say, “I am ignorant,” so instead, Socrates says he has a certain kind of human wisdom. The Apology is the only place I know where Socrates ascribes wisdom to himself. That wisdom is of the situation, saying, Let me explain what’s been going on. I can tell you who I really am, I can tell you what I’m really being accused of. I understand all this very well. That’s not an ignorant mode. There’s a wrinkle in that he claims, I don’t claim to know things I don’t know, which is not a humble confession.

I see The Apology not as a humble or ignorant text, but a self-glorifying one. The Chaerephon oracle story places him in conversation with Oedipus: Socrates gets some information from an oracle that he finds incredible, he can’t believe that it’s the truth, so he decides he has to resist the oracle and spends the rest of his life doing it. The Oedipus story concludes that you can’t fight the oracle, human beings are playthings of the gods, life is tragic, and you should give up now because you have no knowledge. The Socratic version of that story has a very different moral, which is that you can live a happy life and live well by not assuming that you understand the oracle and what it means. You can fight it by trying to investigate and decipher its riddle, even if you’re ignorant, and you don’t blow up your life. The Apology is Socrates saying, I’m ignorant, and I lived a pretty good life. It’s kind of a boast.

You’re reminding me of a previous guest, Sheila Heti, who described the interview as a practice of consulting oracles. She stopped wanting to do interviews when she could no longer imagine her subjects as oracular speakers, becoming more interested in the prophecies issued from her own mind as opposed to from the mouths of others. That’s when she started interviewing AI chatbots instead of people. I just want to hear your reaction to that. I’m not quite sure how to put your understanding, from a set of ancient texts, of consulting the oracle as a way to not blow up your life alongside Sheila’s very contemporary sense that the oracles have nothing left to say, so there’s no point in even asking.

There’s an important detail I left out, which is that Oedipus goes to the oracle and asks, Who are my mother and father? And the oracle responds, You’re going to kill your father and marry your mother. He doesn’t notice that he didn’t get an answer to his question, so he runs away from home thinking he’ll avoid his fate. When Chaerephon comes back to Socrates and tells him that the oracle said there was no one wiser than him, Socrates still thinks, I am not wise. That is the Harry Potter moment that we’ve all been waiting for our whole lives, when some divine source tells you that even though it might not appear that way, you’re secretly a lot wiser than everyone around you. The degree to which the human soul longs for that experience makes it almost unbelievable that when faced with such a declaration, Socrates thinks that the oracle must be wrong. The difference between Socrates and Oedipus lies in whether they have decoded what the oracle has said. The question, “Are there oracles?” is really a question about us, what decoding we are prepared to do, and what things we feel we can take at face value. The speech of AIs seems to require remarkably little decoding.

In some ways, it’s the opposite of what Socrates says about interrogating the poets, who he says “are like diviners or soothsayers who also say many fine things, but do not understand the meaning of them.” Anyone who’s done an author event with a poet knows how true this is. Socrates goes on to say that even the good artisans fall into the same error as the poets, because “they were good workmen, they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters, and this defect in them overshadowed their wisdom.” Part of the practice of the interview, as he’s conducting them to understand the distinctiveness of his own wisdom, seems to be to differentiate between things like genius and inspiration and the high matters, which require understanding—as opposed to simply producing—beautiful things. Is that a fair way of describing the way he’s using the interview to understand his own distinctiveness?

I taught a class last quarter on literary modernism, and we read Hermann Broch, and in one of his novels there is a discussion about the relationship between the aesthetic and the ethical that made a big impression on me. It postulates that it’s important to us to see the work of art, in some substantial way, as a thing that the artist made. We really want to see art as the externalization of something in the artist. Here, Socrates is challenging that. He’s essentially saying a work of art is an accident. He argues that some people are empty vessels who accidentally produce amazing things sometimes. It’s a serious diss to artists. The way he knows is that, if there were anything intentional in there, they would be able to say something about where the art came from. If you ask them about it, what comes out of their mouths is garbage, that is evidence for the disconnect between the aesthetic and the ethical.

Part of the question running through The Apology is the public-versus-private dimension of the Socratic interview. I’m curious to hear you speak a little bit about the relationship of privacy versus publicity to the aims of the Socratic interview.

When Socrates says, I have not lived a public life, what he means is he didn’t try to steer the city in the assembly. But in many ways, these conversations were public, and that’s exactly what he’s on trial for. People liked Socrates humiliating some famous guy. A big part of what these people objected to is that they were being shown up publicly. Think of The Symposium. It’s private in a way, but the whole beginning of the dialogue is how the story got around. There’s something odd about the public-private distinction when applied to Socrates. To the extent that he was magnetic and unavoidable and entrancing, that’s part of what made him threatening.

He must walk this fine line between privacy and publicity, so that he’s being instructive but not punitive, because part of the charge that he brings against his accusers is, If you really thought I was corrupting the youth, you’d understand that I was doing it inadvertently, and if you knew I was doing it inadvertently, then you would know that it would be wrong to put me on trial. You would have approached me and admonished me privately.

That’s right. He thinks he’s admonishing people privately. He’s not admonishing them in the assembly or in the courts. He’s admonishing them in their homes, or in the home of someone they’re staying with, or outside the steps to the courthouse. In that sense, it’s private, but it is not.

What is at stake in setting up the terms on which one has the conversation in front of the semipublic, semiprivate audience, as opposed to doing it truly privately?

There are dialogues that are totally private, no one’s watching. But it’s made clear. Socrates says things like, I wouldn’t say this if anyone could hear what I’m saying to you.What is remarkable about the Socratic dialogues is how much in those conversations, even when there’s an audience, is a negotiation over what we’re doing by having this conversation. I think that’s interesting, because it’s not so true of us today. Renegotiation happens, but not, “Let’s have this conversation in a different way.” Socrates was introducing a new game, and teaching people the rules as they were playing. He must constantly show how people are doing it wrong, which isn’t just a matter of saying, “Your views are false,” it’s a matter of saying, “You don’t know what it is to answer a question.” The stuff that would be relegated behind the scenes is just part of the scene, because there’s nothing they could agree to; these people don’t know what he’s doing.

My favorite moment of renegotiation is at the beginning of The Symposium, when Agathon says, If you sit close enough to me, wisdom can pour from your mind into my mind, like water through cheese cloth. Socrates is like, No I’m good, we’re going to do this through a particular discursive mode, because you can’t pour wisdom from one person’s mind into another by mere proximity.

The moment after Socrates is convicted I find extremely moving. He says, Do not think of my conviction as evidence of the failure of my speech. He means that the deficiency that led to his conviction was not a deficiency of words. He goes on to say, “I had not the boldness or impudence or inclination to address you as you would have liked me to do, weeping and wailing and lamenting, which are things that you have been accustomed to hear from others, and which, as I maintain, are unworthy of me.” What is, for him, the role of passion in the Socratic interview?

Socrates is very self-aware and explicit about the fact that he is not doing what people would normally do in his situation: crying and bringing his family to cry. That is the biggest part of him conducting this interview on philosophical terms. It is related to what he says in Plato’s Gorgias, which is that oratory has no use, and that you should never use flattery for any purpose. He thinks that when you play on people’s emotions, it’s a form of flattery.

Say he were to come before the jury with tears shining down his face, saying, “Please save my life.” He would be relying on the jurors feeling good about themselves if they let him go. They could then have a conception of themselves as good and empathetic people, and he’d be feeding into that. Flattery is a way to force people to do what you want them to do, but not get them to notice, because the pleasure that they feel in the experience covers the use of force. Socrates thinks that’s bad, and you should never do it.

In thinking of these dialogues as interviews, are you trying to rehabilitate Socrates?

I am trying to push back against a conception of the purely negative Socrates. I wouldn’t call that rehabilitation, because a lot of people love that Socrates and some people find him really annoying. I’m sad that I didn’t wear the pants that I made for my book tour that have many of Socrates’ views on them, like “Everyone desires the good,” “It’s better to have injustice done to you than to do injustice,” “There’s no such thing as weakness of will,” “Virtue is knowledge,” etc. People ask, “Didn’t Socrates just not think anything, and wasn’t he just arguing?” The thought that Socrates just refutes people is wrong. But the interesting thing is that his midwifery amounted to extracting those views from the most reluctant mouths.

Where do you get the view that it’s better to have injustice done against you than to do injustice? You get it out of Polis. Where do you get the view that you should exercise self-restraint and not pursue pleasure excessively? You get it out of Callicles. Those are the people he had to refute to get it. He is delivering these idea-babies right from people, because there’s only one way for the conversation about virtue to go. There’s only one set of ways for it to make sense. Part of why I want to recover that is not just to rehabilitate Socrates, but because I think those views are compelling. We don’t want to lose Socratic intellectualism. It’s an ethical theory worth considering that gets obscured with the image of Socrates as a skeptic.

Is there anxiety about how his iconicity gets in the way of the work that he’s doing in the Socratic dialogues?

He seems worried about the icon of Socrates in The Apology.  I wonder who’s worried about it, Socrates or Plato. You must ask yourself the question, “Why is Socrates famous?” If it’s 399 BCE, the answer isn’t Plato yet. It’s Aristophanes. It’s arguable that Socrates’ fame and the kind of persona that appears in the dialogues is due to Aristophanes. There’s a little competition between Plato and Aristophanes about who discovered Socrates. I read that into The Apology. It’s Plato saying, “That old one was totally wrong, but this new one that I’m giving you, this is Socrates.” But there are so many texts where Socrates will say things like, “I just don’t care what people think about me.” The thought that Socrates would care about how his icon is fashioned seems strange to me, but the thought that Plato would care is not strange.
